Standard ACLs match on source address only (ranges 1-99, 1300-1999); Extended ACLs match source and destination address, transport protocol and port (ranges 100-199, 2000-2699)
The default wildcard mask for a standard ACL is 0.0.0.0, meaning an individual host

more.text: Extended ACLs have no default — you must use the "host" keyword or type 0.0.0.0 explicitly for a single host.

sides.text: Named ACLs begin with "ip access-list" instead of "access-list", and can also be referenced by name instead of number

more.text: Numbered ACLs now also support injecting new ACEs, a feature that started as named-ACL-only.

sides.text: Applying an ACL to an interface
ip access-group ID in/out — an ACL has no effect until applied this way

more.text: Only one ACL per interface per direction, but you can have an inbound and outbound ACL on the same interface simultaneously (just not two inbound or two outbound).

sides.text: Read top to bottom; as soon as a rule matches, its permit/deny action is applied and no further rules are checked

more.text: Getting the order of rules right is critical — a more specific deny must come before a broader permit that would otherwise match first.

sides.text: Every ACL ends with an implicit "deny any" — if an ACL is applied to an interface, any traffic not explicitly permitted is dropped

more.text: If no ACL is applied at all, all traffic is allowed by default.

sides.text: Access Control Entries are automatically numbered in increments of 10

more.text: New ACEs can be inserted between existing ones (e.g. ACE 15 between 10 and 20) without rewriting the whole ACL.

sides.text:
eq (equal to)
ne (not equal to)
lt (less than)
gt (greater than)
range (a range of ports, e.g. range 1024-11100)

more.text: Common port names like "www" can be used in place of numbers.

sides.text: Maintains a connection table tracking the two-way state of traffic passing through it

more.text: Return traffic matching an entry in the connection table is permitted by default, even if a rule would otherwise block traffic in that direction.

sides.text: Unlike a stateful firewall, a router ACL does not maintain a connection table and only affects traffic in one direction at a time

more.text: If an ACL is applied outbound only, return traffic is allowed since all traffic is allowed by default when no ACL applies to it. If ACLs are applied in both directions, explicit entries are needed to permit both the outbound and the return traffic.

sides.text: Inside and outside zones classify hosts by interface, with outside-to-inside traffic typically blocked except for return traffic

more.text: A DMZ (demilitarised zone) gives limited, controlled access to servers that need to be reachable from the public Internet.

sides.text: Performs deep packet inspection up to Layer 7 using Application Visibility and Control, for finer-grained traffic classification than port numbers alone

more.text: Can run several security services together (e.g. Advanced Malware Protection) and filter URLs using a database of domain reputation scores.

Better than a standard IPS at filtering and prioritising events, using awareness of hosts on the network (OS, enabled services, traffic patterns) and reputation-based filtering. Cisco Talos Intelligence Group maintains the reputation databases NGFW and NGIPS rely on.

sides.text: Monitors and restricts Layer 2 traffic on a switch port by maintaining a list of authorised source MAC addresses and limiting how many can use the port

more.text: A violation occurs when an unauthorised source MAC appears, or when the port's maximum allowed addresses is reached.

sides.text:
switchport mode must be explicitly access or trunk (no DTP)
switchport port-security enables it
switchport port-security maximum n sets the limit (default 1)
switchport port-security mac-address sets a static allowed MAC
switchport port-security mac-address sticky learns addresses dynamically and stores them in the running-config

Shutdown (default): puts the port into err-disabled state
Restrict: drops offending traffic, logs the violation, increments the counter, keeps the port up
Protect: drops offending traffic, but doesn't log or count it, keeps the port up
Classifies switch ports as trusted or untrusted and inspects traffic on untrusted ports to detect DHCP spoofing, keeping a binding table of which MAC was assigned which IP

more.text: On trusted ports, DHCP messages pass unfiltered; on untrusted ports, messages from a DHCP server are always dropped, and client messages are checked against the binding table.

sides.text:
ip dhcp snooping (global)
ip dhcp snooping vlan n
ip dhcp snooping trust (per interface, typically toward the DHCP server or another switch)

more.text: Can be CPU-intensive, so rate limiting incoming DHCP messages per interface is advisable.

sides.text: Prevents ARP poisoning (a host tricking others into associating its MAC with a victim's IP) by validating ARP messages against the DHCP Snooping binding table

more.text: Static entries must be added, or ports trusted, for hosts with a static (non-DHCP) IP address, since they won't appear in the binding table.

sides.text:
ip arp inspection vlan n (global)
ip arp inspection trust (per interface)
ip arp inspection validate [dst-mac] [src-mac] [ip] for extra validation steps

more.text: Like DHCP Snooping, can be rate limited to protect switch CPU.

sides.text: Protect drops offending frames silently. Restrict drops and logs. Shutdown err-disables the port (default)

Authentication (verifying identity)
Authorisation (deciding permissions)
Accounting (recording actions)
TACACS+ is Cisco-proprietary, runs on TCP port 49, and is often used for centralised CLI access management with granular permissions

more.text: RADIUS is standards-based, uses UDP ports 1812/1813, traffic is optionally encrypted, and is often used for centralised management of normal user access such as a remote access VPN.

sides.text: Authentication: who you are. Authorization: what you may do. Accounting: what you did
WPA used TKIP (deprecated). WPA2 uses AES-CCMP. WPA3 uses SAE, adds forward secrecy and protected management frames

more.text: Personal: shared passphrase. Enterprise: 802.1X with RADIUS.

sides.text: WPA3-Personal replaces the PSK exchange with SAE, resisting offline dictionary attacks. OWE encrypts open networks
Configure a WLAN with WPA2-PSK in the GUI
WLANs, Create New, enter SSID, then Security, Layer 2: WPA+WPA2, AES, PSK, passphrase, Apply

more.text: Make sure the WLAN is enabled and mapped to the right interface.

sides.text: A client must be authenticated to associate with an AP; encryption is separate and governs whether it can actually exchange messages afterwards

more.text: WPA1/2/3-Personal uses open authentication (any client can associate) but requires a pre-shared key to negotiate encryption keys before communication works.

sides.text: A checksum carried in wireless frames that lets the receiver detect if a message was corrupted or maliciously altered

more.text: If the MIC computed by sender and receiver don't match, the frame is dropped.

sides.text: WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) is deprecated and no longer secure

more.text: Shared key authentication (AP sends a challenge, client responds using a matching pre-shared key) is even less secure than open authentication with WEP, since it generates traffic useful for cryptanalysis.

sides.text: AP uses open authentication to begin the connection, but the client (called a supplicant) must then authenticate with an Authentication Server before reaching the rest of the network
Early Cisco-proprietary method, used with WEP; a dynamic, frequently-changed WEP key attempted to work around WEP's weaknesses

more.text: WEP is fundamentally broken and no amount of alteration fixes it — LEAP is now as deprecated as WEP.

sides.text: Cisco-proprietary; the Authentication Server generates a Protected Access Credential (PAC), shared with the supplicant, which they use to authenticate each other and build a TLS tunnel

more.text: The TLS tunnel is then used to authenticate the end user, e.g. via username and password.

sides.text:
PEAP: the AS presents a signed certificate; once verified, a tunnel is built for authentication via MSCHAPv2 or GTC
EAP-TLS: same idea as PEAP, but the client also needs a certificate, usually requiring a full PKI

WPA: uses TKIP, a stopgap for WEP-era hardware, now deprecated
WPA2: uses CCMP (AES counter mode + CBC-MAC for MIC), still secure
WPA3: uses GCMP (AES counter mode + Galois MAC), the most secure, relatively new

None (disabled)
IPSec (client establishes an IPSec tunnel)
VPN Passthrough (client establishes a VPN tunnel to a defined server)
Web Authentication (login via webpage, common for Guest WLANs)
Web Passthrough (agree to conditions via webpage, common for Guest WLANs)
Cisco-proprietary fast-rekeying method that speeds up roaming between APs

more.text: Used with 802.1X, it avoids the need to re-authenticate with the RADIUS server on every roam.
